summary:
Cooper is a decision-support web app that helps Uruguayan farmers compare crop rotations using NASA Earth observation data, built for the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge.

The farmer marks their field on a map and says which rotation they use today and what matters most: saving water, soil health, income, forage or climate resilience. Cooper downloads 30 years of daily NASA POWER climate data and 30 m NASA SRTM elevation for that spot, then simulates every rotation in its library. It shows three side by side: the current one and the two best alternatives, each with five scores, a month-by-month calendar, the supporting data and the risks to review with an agronomist.

It also shows when crops go thirsty, a calendar of heat, frost and heavy-rain risk, how the local climate has shifted since 1996, and maps of erosion (RUSLE), wetness and frost-prone low spots inside the field. A slider recalculates everything with less rain or more heat.

No AI makes the decisions: every result comes from published formulas and written rules anyone can check. AI is limited to language: "Explain it simply" narrates the result over a 3D model of the field, and "Ask Cooper" answers questions by text or voice, in English or Spanish, in the app or on WhatsApp.

Cooper is tuned to Uruguay's farming year, crops and no-till practice, opens offline after the first visit, and exports to PDF and Excel. It helps farmers think; the decision stays with them.
details:
BENEFITS

- Turns 30 years of NASA data into a comparison a farmer can read in minutes.

- Every result is traceable: published formulas and written rules, with no black box.

- "Explain it simply" narrates the analysis aloud over a 3D model of the field for people with no technical background.

- "Ask Cooper" answers questions by text or voice note in English or Spanish, and is also reachable on WhatsApp.

- Opens offline after the first visit and exports reports to PDF, Excel, CSV and JSON.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want farmers to arrive at the conversation with their agronomist better informed: seeing how a different rotation could reduce water stress, keep the soil covered and lose less of it to erosion, and cope with a drier or hotter climate. Cooper helps farmers think; the decision stays with them.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, pandas, NumPy, httpx, pytest.

- Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet (maps), Chart.js (charts), Three.js (3D field) and a service worker for offline use.

- NASA data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and GPM-IMERG), SRTM elevation via OpenTopoData, MODIS NDVI via NASA GIBS.

- Other data: ISRIC SoilGrids, ESA WorldCover, Esri World Imagery, Open-Meteo forecasts.

- AI, for language only: Groq language models and Whisper transcription, ElevenLabs voices.

- Messaging and infrastructure: Twilio WhatsApp, AWS Lightsail, nginx, GitHub Actions for tests and automatic deployment.

CREATIVITY

- The field becomes a 3D scene built from its real SRTM terrain: crops change month by month, soil is coloured by erosion, and the soil washing downhill is proportional to the tonnes lost.

- The narrated story adapts to each field: extra chapters appear only when the data call for them, so two fields get different explanations.

- AI is kept on a short leash: when a language model rewrites the narration, every sentence must keep exactly the same numbers or it is discarded.

- The same explanation reaches farmers where they already are, including a WhatsApp chat.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: no AI makes decisions, and each suggestion states its data, its gaps and its risks.

- Local agronomy: a May-to-April farming year, Uruguayan crops, pastures and crop-pasture rotations, no-till assumed, and pasture rotations suggested only to farmers with livestock.

- Honesty about limits: climate data has a ~50 km grid, soil erodibility is a typical value rather than a measurement, income is relative with no prices or costs, and thresholds still need validation by local agronomists.

- Rural connectivity: offline use, a phone-friendly layout and a browser-voice fallback.

- Privacy: fields and analyses are stored in the farmer's browser, and coordinates are never sent to the AI services.

- Openness: crop, rotation and recommendation tables are plain JSON files an agronomist can correct without touching code.

NASA SRTM Global 1 arc-second elevation (SRTMGL1 v003)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services), MODIS Terra NDVI 8-Day layer
